## C140 — A local-duration probe that lands after a skip writes the previous track's length onto the current one, and persists it

- **Round:** 6 · **Severity:** low _(was medium; verifier narrowed reachability to the gapless-advance path)_ · **Verdict:** **CONFIRMED** _(verify pass, round 6; different agent than the raiser)_
- **File:** `Sources/VellumMusicKit/Playback/PlaybackEngine.swift:2945–2957`; helpers at `:1282–1292`

```swift
        } else if duration <= 0, item.asset is AVURLAsset,
                  let urlAsset = item.asset as? AVURLAsset, urlAsset.url.isFileURL,
                  probingLocalFileURL != urlAsset.url {
            probingLocalFileURL = urlAsset.url
            let fileURL = urlAsset.url
            Task {
                let probed = await LocalMediaDuration.seconds(at: fileURL)
                guard probed > 0 else { return }
                duration = probed
                localFileDuration = probed
                persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded(probed)
                patchActiveQueueTrackDuration(probed)
            }
        }
```

**Problem.** **Every other deferred write in this file is guarded** by `isPlaybackEpochCurrent(epoch)` or
a track-id compare — `probeDeliveredFormat`, `scheduleNowPlayingArtworkLoad`, `loadLyrics` — and this one
is not. `asset.load(.duration)` on a local FLAC/ALAC is a real suspension, and `teardownPlayer()` resets
`probingLocalFileURL = nil` so a new probe is allowed per track. Interleaving: offline track A (no server
duration) starts and its probe begins → the user skips to offline track B (also no duration) → probe B
begins → **probe A completes** and sets `duration` to A's length under B's title, writes A's duration into
`OfflineDownloadManager`'s record for **B** (since `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded` reads `activeTrack?.id`
at completion), and patches `queue[currentIndex]` — B — with A's duration. The scrubber then shows the
wrong length, and B's persisted offline record stays wrong, because `patchActiveQueueTrackDuration`'s
`guard track.duration <= 0` now fails and it will never be re-probed. This is exactly the
offline-download case the code comment says the probe exists for.

**Fix.** Capture `let epoch = playbackEpoch` and `let trackId = track.id` **before** the `Task`, and after
the await `guard self.isPlaybackEpochCurrent(epoch), self.currentTrack?.id == trackId else { return }`.
Pass `trackId` explicitly into `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded(trackId:seconds:)` rather than reading
`activeTrack` at completion time.


**Verified —** **The "every other deferred write is guarded" premise was checked and is true** — `probeDeliveredFormat` guards on epoch, `scheduleNowPlayingArtworkLoad` on a cancelled handle plus track id, `loadLyrics` on track id (with a comment explaining why not epoch), and the next-item staging task on generation + queue index + track id. **This probe is genuinely the sole unguarded deferred write in the file**, which is the strongest part of the entry.

**Four corrections, and they narrow it to low.**
1. **The re-probe blocker is the wrong line.** The entry blames `patchActiveQueueTrackDuration`'s `guard track.duration <= 0`. The actual blocker is one line earlier in the tick: the stale write sets `localFileDuration = probed`, and the `if localFileDuration > 0` branch at **`:2939`** short-circuits the whole chain so B's own probe never starts. An implementer would look at the wrong guard.
2. **The outcome is one of three orderings and one self-heals.** If A's probe lands after B's own probe started, B's later probe **overwrites the offline record with the correct value** and only the in-memory Track stays wrong. A third, worse ordering the entry does not describe: A's probe landing in the gap between teardown and `startCurrentItem`'s `guard let activeTrack` makes the patched Track what `loadAVPlayerItem` reads, so `resolvedDuration` becomes A's value and **A's duration is persisted for B permanently**.
3. **Reachability is much narrower than "the offline-download case".** The branch needs `duration <= 0` at tick time, but `loadAVPlayerItem` already resolves duration **twice** before attach (`LocalMediaDuration.seconds(at:)` for any file URL, then `seconds(asset:)`). The live path is the **OS gapless advance**, which runs no `LocalMediaDuration` probe — so the population is: gapless advance onto a downloaded file whose `Track.duration` is 0 *and* whose pre-rolled item duration has not resolved, plus a skip inside the probe's latency.
4. **Drift:** "exactly the offline-download case the code comment says the probe exists for" is unsupported — **there is no comment on the probe.** The only comment in range is `:2940`, attached to the `localFileDuration > 0` branch and about `AVPlayerItem.duration` being briefly wrong. Delete that sentence.

**Fix is correct and matches the file's three existing patterns**, with two additions: `patchActiveQueueTrackDuration` also reads `currentIndex` at completion and needs the same treatment, and `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded` has **two other callers** (`:2581`, `:2943`) that a signature change touches.


**Re-verified (T238) —** independent second pass, agent 52, judged from the source with the first pass's verdict withheld.

- **Problem:** REAL · **Fix:** ADEQUATE
- **Evidence:** In `periodicTimeObserverTick`, the local-duration probe branch (`probingLocalFileURL != urlAsset.url`) launches `Task { ... duration = probed; persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded(probed); patchActiveQueueTrackDuration(probed) }` with no epoch or track-id capture/guard, unlike every other deferred write in the file. `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded` reads `activeTrack?.id` at completion time (`guard seconds > 0, let trackId = activeTrack?.id else { return }`) and `patchActiveQueueTrackDuration` reads `queue[currentIndex]` at completion time — both "current" state, not the state when the probe started — while `teardownPlayer()` resets `probingLocalFileURL = nil` so a fresh probe starts per track, confirming the cross-track race is reachable.
- **Better approach:** The proposed epoch+trackId guard is directionally correct and matches the file's existing pattern, but `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded` has two other call sites (`resolvePlaybackDuration` at ~1241/1250/1259, and `periodicTimeObserverTick`'s `newDuration` branch at ~2943) that a signature change to `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded(trackId:seconds:)` must also update; the fix as written doesn't call this ripple out.
- **Versus the first pass:** AGREE — the recorded block reaches the same verdict: "Fix is correct and matches the file's three existing patterns, with two additions: `patchActiveQueueTrackDuration` also reads `currentIndex` at completion and needs the same treatment, and `persistOfflineDurationIfNeeded` has two other callers... that a signature change touches."

## C141 — The acquisition completion loop polls for a minute against a captured client and can add tracks to the wrong account

- **Round:** 6 · **Severity:** medium · **Verdict:** **CONFIRMED** _(verify pass, round 6; different agent than the raiser)_
- **File:** `Sources/VellumMusicKit/App/AppModel.swift:1067–1070, 3107, 3124–3128`

```swift
        acquisition.onJobFinished = { [weak self] job in
            guard let self else { return }
            Task { await self.handleAcquisitionJobFinished(job) }
        }
```
```swift
        guard let lib = activeLibrary else { return }
        // … (elided: scan trigger and query construction, 3108-3123)
        for attempt in 0..<20 {
            if attempt > 0 { try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(3)) }
            let query = [artist, title].filter { !$0.isEmpty }.joined(separator: " ")
            let results = (try? await lib.searchCatalog(query: query, limit: 30)) ?? .empty
```

**Problem.** The task is unstructured, never stored and never cancelled, and the loop runs for **up to
20 × 3 s** against the `lib` it captured at entry — with `try? await Task.sleep` discarding
`CancellationError` and no `isSignedIn` / `activeLibrary === lib` check per iteration. If the user signs
out during that minute (`signOut` nils `navidrome`/`jellyfin` at `:1380–1381` but cannot reach this
task) or switches server, the loop keeps polling the **old** client; on a match it calls
`finalizeAcquisitionCatalogAlbum` → `addAlbumToLibrary`, which reads `libraryMagicPlaylistId` and
`activeLibrary` *at that moment* — i.e. it writes **server A's track ids into whichever account is now
signed in**. That is the same cross-account bleed **C21** describes, on a path C21 does not cover.

**Fix.** Store the tasks (`acquisitionCompletionTasks[job.id]`), cancel them in `signOut()` and on
backend switch, and inside the loop replace `try? await Task.sleep` with
`do { try await Task.sleep(…) } catch { return }` plus `guard isSignedIn, activeLibrary === lib else
{ return }` before each attempt.


**Verified —** `signOut` was read in full: it cancels exactly **two** things — the membership auto-sync and the playlist-rows warmup — and **cannot reach this task**, which is created inline, never stored, never cancelled (`onJobFinished` is assigned once, in `init`). Nothing makes the loop exit: `try? await Task.sleep` discards cancellation (moot, since nothing cancels it), `lib` is a **strong** capture so nilling the client does not invalidate it, and there is no `isSignedIn` / identity / generation check anywhere in the loop. *(Inference, well-grounded: Subsonic salted-token auth is stateless and `KeychainStore.clear()` invalidates nothing server-side, so the captured client keeps succeeding against server A for the full minute.)* **The "polls a dead client for up to a minute" half is certain.**

**The wrong-account WRITE needs a tighter window than the entry states.** A bare sign-out makes it a **no-op**: both `addSongToLibrary` and `addAlbumToLibrary` open with `guard let playlistId = libraryMagicPlaylistId`, which `signOut` nils. **The bleed requires sign-out *plus* sign-in to a different account with `refreshLibraryMembership()` resolved, all inside the ~57 s budget.** Once that holds the mechanism is worse than described: `finalizeAcquisitionCatalogAlbum` fetches the tracklist through the captured `lib` (server A) while `addAlbumToLibrary` re-reads `activeLibrary` (account B), so **A's track ids are POSTed to B's playlist through B's client** — and because the local mutation happens *before* the server call, if the server no-ops rather than erroring, `persistLibraryMembershipPayload()` writes A's ids into **B's magic-playlist comment**. Lead with the certain half and scope the bleed.

**Not a duplicate of C21** — C21's inventory and fix name six other call sites and `handleAcquisitionJobFinished` is in none of them, so C21 as written would leave this path untouched. The right editorial move is to add this site to C21's list, not merge the entries.

**Fix guidance:** bumping C21's proposed `sessionGeneration` and checking it before each attempt is **strictly better than storing task handles** — it covers backend switch, sign-out and sign-in with one mechanism and no lifetime bookkeeping to keep correct in two places. If handles are used anyway, they need removal on completion or they leak an entry per job; and `activeLibrary === lib` requires `MusicLibraryProviding` to be class-constrained for `===` to compile — verify that or compare a stored server identity instead.


**Re-verified (T238) —** independent second pass, agent 52, judged from the source with the first pass's verdict withheld.

- **Problem:** REAL · **Fix:** ADEQUATE
- **Evidence:** `handleAcquisitionJobFinished` does `guard let lib = activeLibrary else { return }` once, then loops `for attempt in 0..<20 { if attempt > 0 { try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(3)) } ... let results = (try? await lib.searchCatalog(...)) ?? .empty }` with no `isSignedIn`/`activeLibrary === lib` recheck per iteration, and the task from `acquisition.onJobFinished = { ... Task { await self.handleAcquisitionJobFinished(job) } }` is never stored or cancelled anywhere, including in `signOut()` (which only nils `jellyfin`/`navidrome`, a strong `lib` capture survives). On a match, `addAlbumToLibrary` independently does `guard let playlistId = libraryMagicPlaylistId, let lib = activeLibrary else { return }` — re-reading current session state rather than the captured `lib`.
- **Better approach:** A session-generation counter (the same mechanism already proposed for C21) checked before each attempt is simpler than a per-job task-handle dictionary: it uniformly covers sign-out, sign-in-to-a-different-account, and backend switch in one place, and avoids the task-handle approach's own leak risk (an entry per job that is never removed on normal completion, only on the rarely-hit cancel paths).
- **Versus the first pass:** AGREE — the recorded block narrows reachability (bare sign-out is a no-op since `libraryMagicPlaylistId` is nil'd; the write-bleed needs sign-out *and* sign-in to a different account within the ~57s window) but confirms the core defect, and independently prefers the session-generation approach: "bumping C21's proposed `sessionGeneration` and checking it before each attempt is strictly better than storing task handles."

## C142 — A scrobble that can never succeed is retried every 60 seconds for the life of the install

- **Round:** 6 · **Severity:** medium · **Verdict:** **CONFIRMED** _(verify pass, round 6; different agent than the raiser)_
- **File:** `Sources/VellumMusicKit/Scrobbling/ScrobbleService.swift:253–276`

```swift
    func processPendingScrobbles() async {
        guard processTask == nil else { return }
        guard let app, let lib = app.activeLibrary, !app.effectiveOfflineMode else { return }
        processTask = Task { @MainActor in
            defer { processTask = nil }
            let queue = store.pending
            for item in queue {
                if Task.isCancelled { return }
                do {
                    try await lib.submitScrobble(trackId: item.trackId, timestamp: item.timestamp)
                    store.removePending(id: item.id)
                    // … (elided: recordCompleted)
                } catch {
                    continue
                }
            }
        }
```

**Problem.** Two lifetime defects. (1) A pending scrobble that can **never** succeed — the track id no
longer exists after a server rescan, a 404, a timestamp the server rejects — is retried by the 60 s
timer **forever**, one network round-trip per dead item per minute for the life of the install, because
nothing counts attempts or expires entries. The queue grows monotonically and only ever drains on
success. (2) `let queue = store.pending` snapshots the list, so a scrobble recorded while a drain is in
flight hits `guard processTask == nil`, returns, and waits for the next timer tick instead of joining the
running pass. The second is self-healing; the first is not.

**Fix.** Add `attempts` to `PendingScrobble`; increment on failure and drop the item (or move it to a
dead-letter list surfaced in Settings → Library & Data) after N attempts or on any 4xx from the server.
Drain with `while let item = store.pending.first(where: { !triedThisRun.contains($0.id) })` rather than a
snapshot, so items added mid-run are handled in the same pass.


**Verified —** Searched and confirmed absent: `PendingScrobble` has **no attempts, no lastAttempt, no expiry**; `ScrobbleStore`'s `completedCap = 500` applies only to *completed*, and **`addPending` is an unconditional append with no cap and no prune**; and `removePending` is called from **exactly one place — line 261, on success** (repo-wide grep; the only other reference to `store.pending` is a read-only count in Settings, which offers no clear action). `signOut` never touches the store, and **`applyTrackIDSwaps` does not remap pending scrobbles** — so the headline example (an id changed by a server rescan) is a genuinely permanent failure, not one the stale-id machinery rescues.

**Permanent failure is deterministically reachable on the primary backend:** `NavidromeClient.submitScrobble` → `subsonicRequest`, which throws on **any** Subsonic error payload, so `scrobble?id=<gone>` returns error 70 → throws → `catch { continue }` → the item stays pending forever. *(Inference: Navidrome returns error 70 for an unknown id rather than accepting silently — standard Subsonic. Jellyfin's `Sessions/Playing` is more likely to accept-and-ignore, so **the affected population is Navidrome-weighted** — worth saying, since it changes who is hit.)* One round-trip per dead item per 60 s tick, and the queue is persisted under `vellumPendingScrobbles` with nothing to prune it.

Claim (2) is correct but **more self-healing than the entry allows** — the *next* completed track re-triggers a full drain including the missed item, so "waits for the next timer tick" is worst-case.

**Three fix corrections an implementer hits cold.** (1) **`PendingScrobble` is `Codable` and persisted in `UserDefaults`**, so adding a non-optional `attempts: Int` fails decoding of every existing queue — and `try?` at the load site turns that into `nil`, **silently dropping the entire pending queue on upgrade.** Declare it `Int?` or write `decodeIfPresent`. This is exactly the migration rule CLAUDE.md states for persisted models. (2) "Drop after N attempts" silently discards listening history — prefer the dead-letter half, surfaced next to the existing "Pending scrobbles" row. And **"drop on a 4xx" is not implementable today**: `subsonicRequest` collapses both the HTTP failure and the Subsonic error into forms carrying no distinguishable status, so either thread the Subsonic `error.code` through or make the policy attempt-count-only. (3) The rewritten drain terminates and is safe against mid-loop mutation, but **must keep the `if Task.isCancelled { return }`** the entry's version omits.

**Severity:** medium is defensible but generous — bounded to one request per dead item per minute while online. **The durable half is the unbounded, un-prunable `UserDefaults` queue; lead with that.**


**Re-verified (T238) —** independent second pass, agent 52, judged from the source with the first pass's verdict withheld.

- **Problem:** REAL · **Fix:** ADEQUATE
- **Evidence:** `struct PendingScrobble: Identifiable, Codable, Equatable` has no attempts/expiry field, and `processPendingScrobbles()`'s catch block is `catch { continue }` — no counting, no removal, no dead-letter, so a permanently-failing item (e.g. Navidrome `subsonicRequest` throwing on any Subsonic error payload for a stale id) is retried by the 60s `timerTask` loop forever. `store.removePending` is called only on success.
- **Better approach:** `PendingScrobble` is `Codable` and persisted via `Self.load` which does `try? JSONDecoder().decode(T.self, from: data)` — adding a non-optional `attempts: Int` would fail decoding of the whole existing array on upgrade, and the `try?` silently turns that into "queue is empty," permanently dropping every pending scrobble. Declare it `Int?`/`decodeIfPresent` (this is exactly the "adding non-optional fields needs a migration story" rule CLAUDE.md states for persisted models). Also, "drop on any 4xx" isn't currently implementable — `subsonicRequest`'s thrown errors carry no distinguishable HTTP/Subsonic status today — so the policy should be attempt-count-only unless that plumbing is added first.
- **Versus the first pass:** AGREE — the recorded block makes the identical two points nearly verbatim: "`PendingScrobble` is `Codable` and persisted in `UserDefaults`, so adding a non-optional `attempts: Int` fails decoding of every existing queue... silently dropping the entire pending queue on upgrade," and "'drop on a 4xx' is not implementable today."

# 12. Run summary and stop condition

## The stop condition that actually fired

**The 6-round hard cap. This run did NOT converge.**

The note's convergence rule is *"stop when two consecutive rounds produce no new CONFIRMED findings."* **That never happened.** Every round produced new surviving findings, including the last:

| Round | Candidates raised | Dropped as duplicates | New entries | Surviving after verify |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 72 | 6 (within-round only) | 66 | **62** |
| 2 | 71 | 10 | 61 | **60** |
| 3 | ~70 | 15 | 55 | **53** |
| 4 | 57 | 11 | 47 | **44** |
| 5 | 67 | 17 (+1 pair merged) | 49 | **47** |
| 6 | 61 | 32 | 29 | **28** |
| **Total** | **~398** | **91** | **307** | **294** |

Round 6 still produced **28 surviving findings, four of them high severity** — including a missing privacy manifest that plausibly blocks App Store submission (**C131**), a tautological guard that hides most of a partly-downloaded album (**C133**), a download queue that silently hangs or permanently fails tracks when the network drops (**C134**), and a double Next tap that can stop playback outright (**C139**).

**What this means: the sweep is not finished.** The duplicate rate did rise sharply in round 6 — 32 of 61 candidates, 52%, against 25% in round 5 — which is the first real evidence of saturation in the surfaces entered so far. But saturation of *entered surfaces* is not the same as exhaustion of the codebase, and round 6's yield was high precisely because it entered six surfaces nothing had touched. On the evidence here, **a round 7 aimed at genuinely new surfaces would still find real material.** Anyone reading this document should treat it as a large, verified sample of this codebase's defects — not as a complete inventory.

## Verdicts

Every one of the **307** findings was verified by a **different agent than the one that raised it**, whose instruction was to refute it.

| Verdict | Count |
|---|---|
| **CONFIRMED** | 218 |
| **REINFORCED** | 76 |
| **DENIED** | 13 |

Denied entries are **kept, not deleted**, so later rounds could dedup against them — which they did.

The 13 denied: **L07, L11, L15, L40** · **E—** (none) · **P01, P21, P27, P39, P48** · **C39, C114, C120, C135**.

## Findings by category

| Category | Total | Surviving | high | medium | low |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Layout & organisation | 49 | 45 | 7 | 22 | 16 |
| Efficiency | 56 | 56 | 9 | 31 | 16 |
| Presentation | 60 | 55 | 7 | 35 | 13 |
| Components & consistency | 142 | 138 | 42 | 53 | 43 |
| **Total** | **307** | **294** | **65** | **141** | **88** |

## What the verify pass actually caught

The denials are load-bearing — each killed a claim that would otherwise have been handed over as fact. Three examples where the verifier was right and the raiser was wrong on a **checkable** point:

- **C114** asserted APFS limits path components to 255 **UTF-8 bytes**. It is 255 **UTF-16 code units** (measured: 255 × `あ` = 765 bytes creates fine; 256 fails). The headline CJK case was arithmetically impossible, and the proposed fix would have truncated legal Japanese album titles.
- **C120** asserted Home's recommendation pool is the first 500 alphabetical albums. `buildHomeTopPicksCandidatePool` draws from recently-added, recently-played and per-genre fetches, and touches `libraryAlbums` only as a documented cold-launch fallback.
- **C135** asserted an unpublished flag leaves every offline indicator stale. An `@Published` write inside the health probe fires *after* the flag is set on every path where the reader could see it.

The verify pass also corrected **many surviving entries' fixes**, several of which would have caused damage if implemented as written — **L44** (pruning against a truncated index would have written deletions to the server), **E51** (decoding six widget bitmaps onto one entry would have guaranteed the extension kill it was meant to prevent), **C106** (the proposed demotion does not touch the header that carries the bug), **C134** (leaving tracks pending would have produced an unthrottled retry loop), and **C99** (host validation would have broken every correctly-configured Navidrome `ShareURL`).

# 13. T238 — independent 50-agent re-verification

Every one of the 307 findings was re-read by a **second, independent agent** that had not seen the
first pass's verdict. Each agent's input file was generated with the `**Verdict:**` marker, the
`**Verified —**` block and the severity re-scope annotations **stripped out**, so the judgment was made
from the source first; only afterwards did the agent open this document to say whether it agreed.

Two questions were judged **separately**, because they are not the same question:

1. **Is the problem real?** — decided from the code, with a self-obtained quoted excerpt as evidence.
2. **Is the proposed fix the best way forward?** — `BEST` / `ADEQUATE` (a better approach exists, named)
   / `WRONG` (would not work, would not compile, or would cause damage).

## Results

| Problem | | Fix | | Versus the first pass | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| REAL | 271 | BEST | 122 | AGREE | 292 |
| PARTLY REAL | 36 | ADEQUATE | 169 | DISAGREE | 15 |
| NOT REAL | **0** | WRONG | 16 | | |

**The two axes behaved completely differently, and that is the finding.** On the problem axis the first
pass holds: nothing was judged NOT REAL and disagreement ran at 15/307 (4.9%). On the fix axis, **only
122 of 307 fixes (40%) are implementable as written** — 169 need a named better approach and 16 would
fail outright. The first pass verified *claims* thoroughly and *remedies* barely at all; several of its
blocks never examined the fix, which is exactly where this pass found the damage.

**The 16 fixes rated WRONG:** C31, C38, C49, C99, C114, C123, E53, L13, L15, L40, L44, L45, P15, P28,
P35, P48. They cluster into four failure types:

- **Would not compile** — L15's deletion range takes out a `private extension View` used at eleven
  sites; P15 wraps `String`-returning call sites in `Text(...)`; C49 would break a nonisolated
  `Equatable.==`; C86's fix (rated ADEQUATE) names properties that do not exist.
- **Would do nothing** — P35's Jellyfin fallback is dead code; C31's `markRequestUnresolved(releaseGroupMBID:)`
  would match nothing because `requestedReleaseIds` is keyed by a different identifier; P48's copy is
  already shipped; C123 leaves the latched intent that causes the reported symptom.
- **Does not meet the standard it invokes** — P28's replacement colours also fail WCAG AA
  (recomputed: `systemGreen` 2.13:1, `systemRed` 3.40:1).
- **Would cause damage** — L44 would prune against a lazily-built, 50k-capped index and write the
  deletions to the user's server; L13's CI guard is inverted and fails on a clean tree; E53 reverses a
  deliberate design choice documented in the host file's own comment.

## The 13 denied entries, re-checked

**5 denials do not hold: L11, P01, P21, P27, C135.** 8 hold: L07, L15, C39, L40, P39, P48, C114, C120.

All five failures share one shape — the first pass refuted the entry's *framing*, verified the
underlying defect was real and the fix sound, and then recorded DENIED anyway. **C135**'s own text ends
"keep the `@Published private(set)` + equality-guard change as low-severity robustness", which is the
entry's fix verbatim, while stamping it denied. **P21** and **P27** are live accessibility defects — a
VoiceOver user cannot dismiss the Now Playing cover, and the A–Z index exposes inert letters — currently
sitting in this document looking settled.

## Evidence the second pass was genuinely independent

Beyond the 15 disagreements, the strongest signal is **convergence on specifics before reading**:
agents independently reproduced the first pass's own corrections in C27, C31, C34, C49, C59, L37, P43,
P44, P57, E52, E53, E54 and C99, and on **C130** a second agent hand-traced the same nine mis-bucketed
genre strings *and* independently rejected the same "last matching word wins" alternative. Two passes
landing on nine specific strings and the same rejected remedy is not echo.

## Document defects found and corrected during this pass

- **L20 carried a verbatim copy of L19's verification** — it was never verified in round 1. Corrected
  in place with an explicit note; its T238 block is its first real verification.
- **Four `Verified` blocks and two `Re-verified` blocks were orphaned** outside their entries (L20, E22,
  P15, C127, C142), caused by an `rfind("\n---\n")` in both apply scripts overshooting past a section
  boundary for any entry that sits immediately before one. All six were moved back into their entries
  and the audit re-run: 307/307 now carry both blocks.
- The round-1 apply script also duplicated the finding id inside every heading, and left L19 with no
  block at all. Both fixed.

## Method notes, including what went wrong

- 52 agents, ~6 findings each. Model mix: **3 Opus** (the 13 denied entries — a wrongly killed finding
  is the most expensive error available), **38 Sonnet** (all 65 high-severity findings plus 162 others),
  **11 Fable** (67 lower-severity findings, judged before the instruction to stop using Fable arrived).
- A session usage limit killed 19 Fable agents mid-run; all of their entries were re-run on Sonnet.
- **Folding results in while agents were still reading this document churned it under them** — one agent
  reported line numbers shifting between greps and had to re-fetch before quoting. Nothing was corrupted
  (agents locate findings by heading, and folds only append inside an entry), but it was avoidable
  friction caused by folding incrementally to guard against another rate-limit interruption.
